title: Voting and Turnout
short: Citizens 18 and older may vote where they are registered; turnout is higher in presidential years than midterms and rises with age, education and interest; rules on registration, voting by mail and identification vary by state.
trouble: Students think turnout is the same in every election. Midterm turnout has usually been well below presidential-year turnout.

blocks.html: You know who may vote from the voting amendments: citizens 18 and older, under rules each state sets. Turnout is the share of eligible people who actually vote, and it varies a great deal.

blocks.cap: Turnout figures are rounded; see the sources.

blocks.html: Why do some people vote more than others? Political scientists find that turnout rises with age, education, income and interest in politics, and with how close and exciting the race is. Presidential races get the most attention, so turnout is higher in those years than in midterms. Rules matter too, and states differ: how and when to register (some states allow registration on Election Day; others close registration weeks before), whether to vote early or by mail, and what identification to show. People disagree about these rules: some stress making voting easier, others stress protecting against errors and fraud, and many want both. Studies of how much each rule changes turnout reach mixed results.

blocks.html: Thinking turnout is about the same in every election. Midterm turnout has usually been well below presidential-year turnout, and local elections on their own dates are often lower still. Check the year: presidential elections fall in years divisible by 4.
